# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 23 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 23 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_023_page_001.jpg

---

## Vision 4, Chapter 2

**1** After passing the beast and going forward about thirty feet, a young woman came to meet me, adorned as if she were coming from a bridal chamber — dressed entirely in white, with white sandals, a veil over her forehead, and a white turban; her hair was white as well. **2** From my earlier visions I recognized her as the Church, and I was filled with joy. She greeted me: "Greetings, man of God!" I returned her greeting: "Greetings, my lady!" **3** She asked me, "Did nothing meet you on the way?" I said, "My lady, such a huge beast — capable of destroying whole peoples — but through the power and mercy of God I escaped it." **4** "You escaped well," she said, "because you cast your care upon God and opened your heart to the Lord, believing that you could be saved through nothing other than through his great and glorious name. Therefore the Lord sent his angel — the one who has authority over the beasts, named Segri — and he shut the beast's mouth so that it could not harm you. You have escaped a great tribulation through your faith and your refusal to waver before such a terrifying creature. **5** Therefore go and tell the Lord's chosen ones about his great deeds, and tell them that this beast is a foreshadowing of the great tribulation that is coming. If you prepare yourselves and repent with your whole hearts before the Lord, you will be able to escape it — as long as your hearts are pure and blameless and you serve the Lord blamelessly for the rest of your days. Cast your cares upon the Lord and he will bear them. **6** Believe in the Lord, you who are double-minded — believe that he can do all things, and that he turns his wrath from you and sends afflictions upon those who doubt. Woe to those who hear these words and disobey! It would have been better for them never to have been born."

---

### Council Notes

The color interpretation of the beast's head (promised in ch. 22) is not given in this chapter — it appears to have been lost in the manuscript tradition or relocated. The focus here is on the pastoral interpretation: the beast = the coming tribulation, and the way to survive it is faith without wavering.

The angel Segri (v. 4) is unique to the Shepherd — a named angelic power with authority over beasts. The name has no clear Semitic etymology; it may be a Romanized or invented name.

The "better not born" formula (v. 6) is used only in the gravest contexts in early Christian literature — for Judas (Mark 14:21) and here for those who knowingly disobey the heavenly message. It underscores the seriousness of the Shepherd's call to repentance.

"Cast your cares upon the Lord" (v. 5) alludes to Psalm 55:22 and 1 Peter 5:7 — the Shepherd is deeply rooted in the broader biblical tradition even as it adds its own distinctive imagery.
